Tenuously means in a way that is weak, fragile, thin, or barely holding together.

When something exists or is done tenuously, it is technically there — but only just barely. It has so little strength, substance, or support that it could easily break apart, disappear, or be proven wrong. Think of a single spider thread stretched between two branches in the wind. It is connected. But the connection is so thin and fragile that you hesitate to even call it one.

That feeling — it's there, but barely, and it could collapse at any moment — is the heart of "tenuously."

It helps to picture a sliding scale of strength:

Strongly → Moderately → Weakly → Tenuously → Not at all

"Tenuously" lives at the extreme thin end. Something done tenuously is one small step away from not existing at all.
The Three Main Ways It's Used

"Tenuously" appears in three broad types of situations:

1. Connections and Relationships

This is the most common use. When two things are tenuously connected, linked, or related, their connection is so slight that it barely qualifies as a connection at all.

  • "The two crimes are only tenuously linked — they happened in the same city, and that's about it."
  • "His new book is tenuously related to his earlier work."

In both cases, a connection exists, but it's so thin that you'd be stretching it to call it meaningful.

2. Arguments, Evidence, and Claims

When a position, theory, or argument is tenuously supported or grounded, it means the backing behind it is flimsy and unconvincing — there might be some evidence, but not nearly enough to hold the claim up firmly.

  • "Her conclusion was tenuously supported by just one unclear data point."
  • "His accusation was tenuously based on rumour and guesswork."

The argument is still being made, but it's standing on very shaky ground.

3. Holding On / Surviving

When someone or something is tenuously holding on, surviving, or maintaining something, it means they are doing so by the thinnest of margins — and could lose their grip at any moment.

  • "After the scandal, she tenuously held on to her position as director."
  • "The old cultural tradition is still tenuously alive in a few remote villages."

Here, the survival or grip is real, but precarious — like holding a heavy bag with just two fingers.

No matter how it's used, "tenuously" always carries these qualities with it:

  • Fragility — the thing could easily break or disappear.
  • Insufficiency — it doesn't have as much strength, substance, or support as it ideally should.
  • A quiet warning — using this word signals that something is technically there, but you probably shouldn't rely on it or take it seriously.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Barely focuses purely on degree — just barely enough. It doesn't say anything about why something is thin.
  • Weakly is more general and physical — done without much force. It doesn't carry the sense of fragility or near-nothingness.
  • Tenuously is more specific and richer. It means something is thin in substance, strength, or integrity — and suggests it could collapse under any real scrutiny or pressure.

Picture a thread so thin it's almost invisible — barely connecting two things. It is a connection, but if you breathe on it too hard, it breaks. That's tenuous. Doing something tenuously means you are doing it in exactly that thread-thin, barely-there way.

You will almost always see "tenuously" paired with words like:

  • tenuously connected / linked / related
  • tenuously held / maintained
  • tenuously supported / grounded / based
  • tenuously alive / surviving

Whenever you see "tenuously" before one of these words, your brain should immediately think: this is barely holding together.
